title: The words of return
hookLine: Adam receives words from his Lord and turns back, and is forgiven (2:37; 7:23)
last: WASWAS — NOT EVERY VOICE IS YOURS.

lines: EXPLAIN IT, OR SAY I WAS WRONG.
cards: A mistake lands, and it's clearly yours. The stomach drop. Then the fork in the road.
One way: explain. It wasn't really my fault. Anyone would have.
The other way: three hard words. I was wrong. One is easier in the moment.
The other is the one people say lets them breathe again afterward. Adam and his wife stand in the garden, covering themselves with leaves. This is their fork.

teach.b: Remember Iblis. When he refused to bow and was sent out, whose fault did he say it was? In surah seven, he says to God: because You have sent me astray.
Now Adam and his wife, in the same surah, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!” No excuse.
No blaming the whisperer, or each other. Surah two tells what happened next: “Then Adam received from his Lord words (of revelation), and He relented toward him.”
Some early commentators say those words were this very prayer: God gave Adam the words to come back with.
The word for it is tawbah, from the root t-w-b, to turn back, to return. And the same root is used for God.

teach.h: AT-TAWWAB — THE ONE WHO TURNS TOWARD.
teach.b: One of His names is at-Tawwab, the One who keeps turning back toward the one who turns. The verse ends: “Lo! He is the Relenting, the Merciful.” So tawbah isn't groveling.

It's two turns: you turn around, and find you're being turned toward. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim pictures it. A man loses his camel in the desert, with all his food and water on it, and lies down to die.

He wakes, and it's standing there. God, the hadith says, is happier with a servant's tawbah than that man is with his camel. And Muslim teachers draw one more thing from this: Adam was forgiven, there and then.
The human story, in Islam, starts with a mistake, and a return that worked.

how: Muslims make tawbah by stopping the wrong, regretting it, resolving not to return to it, and, where someone was harmed, putting it right; many recite Adam's words from 7:23 in their prayers.

o: a set payment that makes up for a broken rule
punishing yourself until all the guilt is gone
turning back to God, and being turned toward

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: in the Qur'an, Adam blames the whisperer
he and his wife say: we have wronged ourselves.
the same root is used for a person's repentance and for God's
t-w-b: tawbah for the one who turns back; at-Tawwab, the One who turns toward.
in the Qur'an, Adam is forgiven
"He relented toward him. Lo! He is the Relenting, the Merciful."

games.q: you're Adam, standing in the garden covered in leaves, and you've just eaten from the one tree. what do you say?
o: we have wronged ourselves; forgive us.
You made the tree too tempting.
games.why: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." and God relented toward him. Iblis, at his fork, had blamed God.

practice: Let one real thing you're sorry for come to mind, from this week or this year, and if an excuse comes with it, set the excuse down.

If you pray, say sorry to God in your own words, as plainly as Adam did; if you don't, say it silently to the person you let down, or just to yourself: I was wrong. Then notice what it feels like to have turned around.

wordCard.voice: Tawbah. Turning back, repentance: you turn toward God, and find God turning toward you.

orig.note: Arabic: repentance, turning back, from t-w-b, to return; God's name at-Tawwab shares the root.

carryVoice: Your line: we wronged ourselves; forgive us. The way back is open from the start. That was day twenty-seven.
